lesson.title: The Great Migration Across a Widening Religious Divide
lesson.summary: Facing intensifying persecution under King Charles I in the 1630s, tens of thousands of English Puritans crossed the Atlantic in a single decade, bringing whole families and congregations to build a religious society in New England.
lesson.body:
Puritans were English Protestants who believed the Church of England, though officially reformed since Henry VIII's break with Rome, still retained too much Catholic ritual, hierarchy, and ceremony. Most Puritans hoped to reform the church from within, but a smaller group known as Separatists concluded the church was too corrupt to reform and broke away entirely to worship independently; it was Separatists of this kind who founded Plymouth Colony in 1620, arriving on the Mayflower and establishing the first permanent English settlement in New England.

Conditions for Puritans in England grew markedly worse after Charles I became king in 1625. Charles favored a high church style of worship closer to Catholic practice, enforced partly through his controversial ally William Laud, who became Archbishop of Canterbury in 1633 and used ecclesiastical courts to punish Puritan ministers and silence dissent. Political tensions compounded the religious pressure: from 1629 to 1640, Charles ruled without calling Parliament at all, a period sometimes called his Personal Rule, during which Puritans lost even the parliamentary voice they had previously used to push back against royal and church policy.

These converging pressures produced what historians call the Great Migration, a roughly decade long wave beginning around 1630 in which tens of thousands of English Puritans left for the Americas, the large majority settling in New England while others went to Puritan controlled colonies in the Caribbean, particularly Providence Island and Barbados. The most significant single expedition sailed in 1630 under John Winthrop, who led a fleet that founded the Massachusetts Bay Colony and served as its governor for much of the following two decades. Winthrop is remembered for a sermon, often called A Model of Christian Charity, in which he described the colony's mission using the phrase city upon a hill, an image meant to convey that the whole world would be watching to see whether this new Christian community succeeded or failed.

The character of this migration distinguished New England sharply from Virginia's earlier settlement. Rather than young single men recruited primarily for labor, Puritan migrants typically traveled as complete family units, and often as entire congregations migrating together under their own minister, bringing an existing social and religious structure with them rather than building one from scratch in the colony. This pattern produced a more balanced, stable population from the outset and helps explain why New England's population grew rapidly through births rather than depending, as Virginia long did, on a constant stream of new arrivals simply to offset high mortality.

The Great Migration slowed abruptly around 1640, and the reason was political rather than economic. The English Civil War broke out that decade between Charles I and Parliament, a conflict in which Puritans held significant power on the parliamentary side, giving English Puritans new hope of reforming their church and government at home rather than fleeing it. Migration to New England never fully returned to its 1630s pace, but by then the Puritan colonies, especially Massachusetts Bay, had already established the population and institutions that would define the region for generations.
